I can just go around the globe, but it doesn't come out well.

background.text: Let me ask you a very specific one, though, because there is a theory going around, you will know the theory I'm talking about, secular stagnation, that there is some long-term issue that growth has in some way run out in the Western world, that technology might have slowed down, there's nothing to invest in, that only the rich people have money to spend and they don't spend it anyway, and that these are all long-term things and there's really no growth left. What weight do you put on that theory?

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: Well, secular stagnation is an old term which was coined by a prominent professor at a major university, in 1938, trying to describe why, after the 1929 crash, it took so long for the American, and in fact the rest of the world, to recover. In fact, in the United States, unemployment stayed in double digits from 1929 until 1938, when, in fact, this professor raised the issue. It's basically, as he put it, that there's something structural, long-term structural, secular, long-term structural, in the system which is preventing it from growing. And indeed, that is a reasonably good characterization of what's going on in the world today, and the only question is, why is it happening?

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: Give us your prognosis for the Eurozone. Those German figures were terrible yesterday. People are beginning to talk again about, actually, did the crisis end in the way that we talked about two years ago?

ground_truth: Well, the problem basically is in the very structure of the eurozone itself. Putting everybody into a single currency makes it very difficult for them to adjust if they had in the past, before they entered the euro, continuously devalued in order to remain internationally competitive. Now, it's true that a remarkable phenomenon occurred. On January the 1st, 1999, all of those countries came together and basically, the way I put it, is that they expected the Italians to behave like Germans. But the cultures between the Germans and the Italians is profoundly difficult to change. And however, the eurozone worked extraordinarily well. For the first eight years. And the reason is that the boom, the so-called dot-com boom was going on, and everybody could be competitive, no matter how poorly they operated. And indeed, Italy was not competitive. Their unit labor costs went up, and that was true of Greece, Portugal, Spain. And the result was that when the crisis hit in 2008, the whole system collapsed and everyone went back to work. They went back to their old problems.
